## Solution

The converse is **false**. I will first verify the forward implication, then exhibit an explicit counterexample to the converse.

### The forward implication holds

Suppose $\sigma\cdot f = -f$ for some $\sigma\in S_n$. Let $H=\langle\sigma\rangle$. Since $\sigma\cdot f=-f$, applying $\sigma$ again gives $\sigma^{2}\cdot f = f$, so the $H$-orbit of $f$ is $\{f,-f\}$ (unless $f=0$, which is trivial). Decompose $S_{n}$ into left cosets $S_n=\bigsqcup_i \tau_i H$. Then

$$n!\,S(f)=\sum_{\tau\in S_n}\tau\cdot f=\sum_i \tau_i\cdot\!\Big(\sum_{h\in H}h\cdot f\Big).$$

The inner sum $\sum_{h\in H}h\cdot f$ equals $\frac{|H|}{2}(f+(-f))=0$ (the orbit is $\{f,-f\}$, each appearing $|H|/2$ times). Hence $n!\,S(f)=0$, i.e. $S(f)=0$. ∎

### The converse fails: a counterexample

Take $n=3$ and $f = 2x_1 - x_2 - x_3 \in \mathbb{Q}[x_1,x_2,x_3]$.

**$S(f)=0$.** For each $\tau\in S_3$, $\tau\cdot f = 2x_{\tau(1)}-x_{\tau(2)}-x_{\tau(3)}$. Summing over all $\tau$, the coefficient of each $x_i$ is
$$2\cdot|\{\tau:\tau(1)=i\}|-|\{\tau:\tau(2)=i\}|-|\{\tau:\tau(3)=i\}|=2\cdot 2 - 2 - 2 = 0.$$
So $\sum_{\tau}\tau\cdot f = 0$, hence $S(f)=0$.

**No $\sigma\in S_3$ satisfies $\sigma\cdot f = -f$.** We have $-f = -2x_1+x_2+x_3$. Checking every element:

| $\sigma$ | $\sigma\cdot f$ | equals $-f$? |
|---|---|---|
| $e$ | $2x_1-x_2-x_3$ | no |
| $(12)$ | $2x_2-x_1-x_3$ | no ($x_1$ coeff. $-1\neq -2$) |
| $(13)$ | $2x_3-x_2-x_1$ | no ($x_1$ coeff. $-1\neq -2$) |
| $(23)$ | $2x_1-x_3-x_2 = f$ | no ($=f\neq -f$) |
| $(123)$ | $2x_2-x_3-x_1$ | no ($x_1$ coeff. $-1\neq -2$) |
| $(132)$ | $2x_3-x_1-x_2$ | no ($x_1$ coeff. $-1\neq -2$) |

Thus no $\sigma\in S_3$ sends $f$ to $-f$, yet $S(f)=0$.

### Conceptual explanation

The map $S$ is the Reynolds operator, i.e. the projection onto the trivial isotypic component of the $S_n$-representation $\mathbb{Q}[x_1,\dots,x_n]$. The condition $S(f)=0$ merely says $f$ has **no trivial component** — it lies in the direct sum of all nontrivial irreducible subrepresentations. The condition $\exists\sigma:\sigma\cdot f=-f$ is far more restrictive: it requires $f$ to be an eigenvector (with eigenvalue $-1$) of *some* group element.

For $n=3$, the degree-$1$ part decomposes as $\mathbf{1}\oplus V$ where $V=\{ax_1+bx_2+cx_3:a+b+c=0\}$ is the $2$-dimensional standard representation. A generic vector of $V$ (such as $2x_1-x_2-x_3$) has $S(f)=0$ but is not an eigenvector of any element of $S_3$ — the transposition $(23)$ fixes it, and the other elements move it to linearly independent vectors. Hence the converse is false in general.

### PROOF COMPLETE
